text: CNOT isn't a one-off trick — it's the first instance of a general recipe: take any single-qubit gate U, and build a two-qubit controlled-U gate that applies U to the target if and only if the control is 1. That recipe is how most two-qubit gates on real quantum hardware get built.

In block form, controlled-U is identity in the top-left block, covering control equals 0, and U itself in the bottom-right block, covering control equals 1. CNOT is exactly this with U equal to X. Plugging in U equal to Z gives controlled-Z, which leaves ket-00, ket-01, and ket-10 untouched and multiplies ket-11 by negative 1. Unlike CNOT, CZ's matrix is symmetric between its two qubits — swapping which one you call the control gives the same gate.

On a lone ket-11, that negative 1 looks like nothing but a harmless global phase. But apply CZ to the uniform two-qubit superposition, all four amplitudes equal to one-half, and only the ket-11 term flips sign, giving the other three terms untouched and ket-11 negated. The measurement probabilities stay at one-quarter each — CZ changes nothing you'd measure directly here — but the relative phase between ket-11 and the rest of the superposition is now real, and it would show up the moment this state meets another interfering gate.

The same block-form recipe builds a controlled version of any single-qubit gate. Controlled-H applies the Hadamard matrix to the target only when the control is 1, useful for conditional superposition generation. Controlled rotation gates do the same with a rotation matrix in that block, and they're the standard building blocks for variational quantum circuits. Every one of these shares the same shape: identity in the control-zero block, the chosen gate in the control-one block.

Next lesson covers two gates that don't fit the controlled-U pattern directly: SWAP, which exchanges two qubits outright, and Toffoli, which extends the controlled idea to two controls at once, giving you a reversible version of classical AND.
